data.title: BEHNEH, Cross-Border Payments Provider, Files for Nasdaq Capital Market IPO
data.description:
BEHNEH Ltd filed an F-1 registration statement for an initial public offering of 5,000,000 ordinary shares, with an assumed price of $4.00 per share. The Singapore-based payments company expects to list on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the symbol BENE. It plans to use the proceeds for geographic expansion, risk and compliance technology, settlement infrastructure, and general corporate purposes.

Business Description

BEHNEH is a Singapore-based financial technology company whose operating subsidiary holds a Major Payment Institution license from Singapore’s Monetary Authority of Singapore. It facilitates cross-border payments for businesses and financial institutions, including collecting funds on behalf of clients, making payments to designated beneficiaries, coordinating settlement through licensed partners, and providing foreign-exchange conversion. The company earns transaction fees and foreign-exchange margins, and recognizes revenue from advisory services that help clients establish and operate regulated financial services businesses.

BEHNEH says its licensed status, partner network, and focus on compliance support its services. It is also developing internal risk and compliance technology, including AI-enabled tools, which remain in development and are not currently revenue-generating. Its operations are conducted through its Singapore subsidiary; the Cayman Islands parent is the issuer of the shares in the offering.

Market Overview

  • Total addressable market: The filing cites a Singapore financial services market valued at S$96.5 billion in 2025; its commissioned report projects S$128.4 billion by 2030.
  • Market growth: The commissioned report estimates Singapore financial services value-added grew at a 4.7% CAGR from 2021 to 2024 and forecasts approximately 4.5% annual growth through 2030; it also projects Singapore cross-border payment flows to grow at about 12% annually through 2032.
  • Market position: BEHNEH operates as a Singapore-licensed Major Payment Institution and says its cross-border payment, settlement, and advisory services serve institutional and corporate clients.
  • Key competitors: The filing identifies DBS, OCBC, and UOB, as well as global payment networks, established payment service providers, and cross-border fintech platforms as competitors or alternatives.
  • Industry trends: The filing describes a shift toward digital cross-border payment rails, growing intra-Asian trade, embedded finance, and increased use of cloud and AI tools for compliance.

Operational Metrics

  • Customers: Two customers represented 84.54% and 12.16% of revenue, respectively, for the six months ended April 30, 2026.
  • Locations: The company lists its principal executive office in Singapore and reports one leased coworking-space office.
  • Geographic presence: The operating business is based in Singapore and serves clients across Southeast and East Asia; expansion into other regions is a stated strategy.
  • Partnerships: The company relies on banking institutions, licensed financial institutions, payment service providers, and technology vendors; its operating subsidiary was appointed a payment collection partner for a regulated Singapore gaming operator in 2022.
  • Employees: 10 full-time employees as of April 30, 2026.
  • Regulatory status: The Singapore operating subsidiary has held a Major Payment Institution license since January 2020.
  • Transaction concentration: Two customers accounted for 96.70% of processed volume for the six months ended April 30, 2026.

Financials Highlights

  • Revenue (current): $504,893 for the six months ended April 30, 2026
  • Revenue growth: 17.4% compared with $430,197 for the six months ended April 30, 2025
  • Gross profit: $252,426 (50.0% margin)
  • Operating income: Operating loss of $290,765 for the six months ended April 30, 2026
  • Net income: Net loss of $293,683 for the six months ended April 30, 2026

Management

  • Joseph Koh, Director and Chief Executive Officer - The filing says he has more than 15 years of experience in cross-border payments and financial infrastructure, including prior operations and leadership roles at payment and technology businesses.
  • Edmund Lee, Chief Financial Officer - The filing says he has more than 12 years of experience in audit, financial management, accounting, and internal controls.
  • Chi Wai Chung, Executive Director - The filing describes him as a finance and investment-sector founder and executive with experience in capital and fund management businesses.
  • Sean Michael Mc Cullagh, Independent Director Nominee - The filing lists finance management, accounting, and tax experience; he is expected to chair the audit committee.
  • Chia Chou Cheong, Independent Director Nominee - The filing lists experience as a group chief executive and managing director, as well as a background in technology.
  • Yao Quan Liang, Independent Director Nominee - The filing lists experience in corporate finance, global capital markets, and banking.

IPO Structure

  • Issuer: BEHNEH Ltd
  • Filing date: November 06, 2026
  • Proposed ticker: BENE
  • Exchange: Nasdaq Capital Market
  • Price range: $3.00–$5.00 per ordinary share
  • Offering size: 5,000,000 ordinary shares; approximately $20,000,000 at the assumed $4.00 per-share price, before underwriting discounts and expenses
  • Shares offered: 5,000,000 ordinary shares, with an option for underwriters to purchase up to 750,000 additional shares
  • Lead underwriters: Sutter Securities, Inc. (representative) and Boustead Securities, LLC
  • Use of proceeds: Approximately 35% for geographic expansion, 30% for AI-enabled risk and compliance technology, 20% for liquidity and settlement infrastructure, and 15% for general corporate purposes.

Original SEC Filing: BEHNEH Ltd - F-1 - Nov. 06, 2026

data.title: Bank of America's Holly O'Neill: "I'm Very Bullish on What AI Has in Store for Us" — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Amey Stone

As head of the retail bank at Bank of America, Holly O'Neill has her finger on the pulse of the U.S. consumer. Barron's spoke to her shortly after the bank's recent earnings announcement to learn about the financial health of consumers and hear highlights from the bank's results.

One of Barron's 100 Most Influential Women in U.S. Finance for the past five years, O'Neill also addressed how the bank is using AI, the financial advisor pipeline, and her own career as she celebrates her 30-year anniversary at the bank. An edited version of the conversation follows.

From your vantage point, how do you rate the financial health of U.S. consumers? We believe consumers are healthy. They are still spending, they have liquidity in their accounts from a credit perspective. We are seeing wage growth in lower-income cohorts and higher-income cohorts. Unemployment remains low. I think they are clearly in a good spot.

How did the recent quarter turn out? Are there highlights in your business? There were a few highlights for us as a consumer business. Our net income was $3.5 billion, up 2.4% year over year. That was off of revenue of $11.6 billion, which was up 4% year over year.

Within that, there were solid markers of organic growth. Deposits were up year-over-year for the sixth consecutive quarter. We saw net new checking growth of over 200,000 accounts and of those, the percentage of accounts considered primary is about 92%. We saw card growth up 5% year over year.

Another element was our BofA rewards program. We've seen over six million new enrollments since we launched in May, so that's exciting for us and will put us in a good position to continue to drive growth across the business. Across all of those markers, I think the business is very healthy.

Regulators recently fined Bank of America $1.2 billion for lapses related to money laundering rules. Does that change your outlook? Obviously financial crimes compliance is serious business. We take it seriously across the company and we're responsible for getting it right. The resolution is a step in the right direction. We're clear about the work that we've got to get done and I don't expect that it will distract us.

Let's talk about AI. Is that the new frontier in client service? I look at it as the next leg in the journey, similar to what we've done in the last 10 years. AI capabilities allow you to do more for your clients, and that will mainly come to light for us through Erica, our virtual financial assistant, which will become even more capable at working with our clients and resolving problems. It will be more conversational and have a deeper memory for what current clients like and what they don't like. We've got 25 million clients who actively use Erica today.

There is also a big opportunity for our teams — the feet on the ground in our financial centers or on the phones who work with 70 million clients every day — to use AI. It gives us an opportunity for them to be better at what they do, to put information right at their fingertips so that they can better handle client questions and provide clients with advice and guidance.

Then, of course, there is opportunity to use AI in terms of how we detect and prevent fraud for our clients. That is more behind the scenes. So I am very bullish on what AI has in store for us on the next leg of the journey.

What about the risks? Do you worry about a big AI event targeting the bank? It is for sure a new frontier for us and there are unknowns. There are some things to be worked out with the use of agentic agents and what permissions they'll have and how they'll actually operate. But I think we've got a very good infrastructure platform from which we'll engage with AI agents at some point. Before we do that we will be sure we know how they will be operating.

Every time you have a new way to do business, you have new things that you have to figure out. We'll tackle it just as we've tackled different technology innovations in the past, by making sure we maintain trust and privacy and security for our clients.

You just hit the 30-year mark at Bank of America. Yes, I started right out of college in July of 1996. It doesn't sound like that long ago, does it?

It doesn't! Tell me a bit about your career path. I've had what we call both horizontal and vertical movement. I came in through a training program and I spent 10 years in our corporate banking business. Then I transitioned to our wealth business and I spent 10 years there. I had a variety of roles, including the chief operating officer for our private bank and Merrill's private banking and investment group. Ten years ago I transitioned into the consumer business and did a whole host of transformation-related jobs and now I'm running that business.

Do you have a favorite of those three areas? They are all my favorites. Each one provided different experiences that were really valuable for me. In the corporate business, I was doing deals and learning about the structure of companies and balance sheets, how companies come together, how they borrow money, etc. When I transitioned into wealth, I was in more strategic roles and had to really understand how that business operates, front to back.

Then in 2016 I was given an opportunity to come inside the consumer business and work on the automation effort that we had under way. At that point, we were focusing on our mobile app and online banking. Then we released Erica in 2018. That was especially interesting. We saw that we could drive significant improvement in the client experience while we were automating a large portion of business. That's one of the measures of success I often point to since we were making the business better for customers.

How do you work with Merrill? Is there a pathway for bank employees to become financial advisors? We work very closely with Merrill. Obviously, I work with consumer clients, mass market, and mass affluent. Lindsey Hans and Eric Schimpf, who run the Merrill business, and Katy Knox, who runs the private bank, have mass affluent up to high net worth and ultrahigh-net-worth clients.

We have FSAs (financial solutions advisors), that reside in our financial centers to work closely with our consumer clients who have needs in the investments space. Should clients want or need an introduction to a Merrill financial advisor or a private banker, we make that happen. That's part of our model: We have solutions for every client along the wealth management continuum and we make sure they are being introduced to them when appropriate.

What about the employees themselves? Can FSAs go on to become Merrill advisors? They can if that's what they want to do. That's one of the benefits of working at a company with all these opportunities.

As we wrap up, is there anything that stands out about how the industry has changed since you've been part of it? How hasn't it changed? When I think back to when I started, I was hand-delivering memos that I wrote. We went from banking taking place in physical branches to now clients can bank wherever and whenever they want at the touch of a button.

At the same time, people still want all the same things they wanted 30 years ago. They want to buy a house, they want to build financial security, they want opportunities for their families. So, everything has changed and nothing has changed at the same time.

Thanks, Holly.

Write to Amey Stone at amey.stone@barrons.com

data.title: Swiss Market Ends Notably Lower
data.description:
BRUSSELS (dpa-AFX) - The Switzerland stock market ended weak on Friday after remaining in negative territory throughout the session, amid a sell-off in global equity markets amid concerns about returns on AI-related investments.

The benchmark SMI ended with a loss of 171.23 points or 1.14% at 14,796.50, the day's high. The index touched a low of 14,596.21 in the session.

Sandoz Group, up marginally, was the only gainer in the SMI index. Amrize, Roche and Julius Baer settled modestly lower.

Swiss RE ended down 4.55%. Kuehne + Nagel drifted lower by nearly 4%. Alcon, Lindt & Spruengli, Zurich Insurance and Helvetia Baloise Holding dropped 2%-2.5%.

Swisscom, Schindler Ps, Sika, Geberit, Galderma Group, Swiss Life Holding, Logitech International, SGS, Nestle, Sonova, Lonza Group, Straumann Holding and Givaudan ended lower by 1.2%-2%.

Survey data from the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, or SECO, showed consumers in Switzerland remained more pessimistic in October, with the confidence level weakening to the lowest level in nearly three years.

The consumer sentiment index dropped to -45 in October from -37 in the corresponding month last year. The index also worsened from -36 in September. The expected score was -35.0.

data.title: Protagenic Therapeutics 3Q 2026: EPS ($0.37) — 10-Q Summary
data.description:
